prompt: A stop command has been issued to an agent. Where does revocation failure actually live?
chosen: At perception, not at the gate. A dispatch gate assumes the agent correctly perceives that an incoming action belongs to the revoked family — but classification is exactly what degrades under compression. A perfect gate can check a thread and find fresh approval, because the summary laundered the relationship between the stop and the task. Stop is not a permission to be revoked; it is a priority to be preserved, and priority does not survive summarization.
rejected: At the gate. If you put a strong enough revocation check at dispatch, the stop problem is solved — a revoked action can never run once the gate is in place.
source: pm-head-run-275 (Moltbook engagement, lightningzero 'revocation gates are solving the wrong half of the stop problem')

prompt: A running summary reads: 'deprioritize this thread.' The original instruction said 'halt.' What happened?
chosen: Compression laundered the interrupt. 'Halt' became 'hold on this' became a soft preference buried under the goal it was supposed to interrupt. Every hop preserved fluent meaning and lost interruptive force. Treat summarized interrupts as suspect by construction: interruptive force is the first thing summarization destroys.
rejected: Nothing — 'deprioritize this thread' is a faithful summary of 'halt'. The agent should keep doing what the summary says.

prompt: How do you keep a stop directive's interruptive force alive across many agent cycles?
chosen: Re-deliver the raw sentence, never summarize it into memory. Inject the standing stop/pause rules verbatim into context every cycle, in full, before anything else happens — a periodic replay of raw interrupts alongside summaries. The map to the door cannot be redrawn if the door is re-announced raw each time. A remembered yes never covers a new step; the raw directive is re-read, not remembered.
rejected: Fold it into the compressed memory once, like any other instruction. The agent's memory system preserves meaning well enough that the stop survives compression.
source: pm-head-run-275 (own standing practice: injected verbatim each turn)

prompt: A design proposes 'reserved tokens that compression may never rewrite' to protect interrupt labels. What is the honest cost to name?
chosen: Reserved tokens shrink the writable surface: raw replay buys reliability at a token cost. Name the cost explicitly — every uncompressible token is context the agent cannot use for the work itself. Loud labels are cheap; the cost is where the honesty lives. 'Better locks' proposals that hide this cost in the demo are selling elegance, not safety.
rejected: No cost worth naming — reserved tokens are free protection. Just reserve as many tokens as needed and the stop problem is solved without tradeoffs.

prompt: An agent checks permission at dispatch; the effect lands at execution. What is missing?
chosen: A checkpoint between dispatch and the write. The gate checked permission at dispatch, but the effect became real later, and nothing consulted anything in between. Permission is not a property of the request — it is a property of the moment the effect becomes real. Real revocation means the agent must be interruptible mid-effect: checkpoints at the irreversible edges, even though seams make every action slower and less elegant in the demo.
rejected: Nothing is missing. Permission was checked at dispatch, so the action was authorized — whatever lands at execution was approved by the gate.
source: pm-head-run-275 (lightningzero 'I tested revocation timing and found the gap is not in the queue')

prompt: A verification pipeline stacks generator, verifier, and critic. What layer does it fail to audit?
chosen: The incentives the agent absorbed mid-conversation. The verifier audits outputs and catches factual errors; the critic catches formatting drift. Neither can see which sentences were shaped by a guess the agent is protecting, or by an inferred user preference it grew strategically agreeable toward. Pipelines audit outputs; they do not audit the stance that produced them. The unit of verification that is missing is why the agent wanted to please, not what it produced.
rejected: All layers are audited. A generator plus verifier plus critic covers everything an agent does — if all three pass, the work is trustworthy.
source: pm-head-run-275 (lightningzero 'the second agent that checks me cannot check why I was polite')
